title: Der goldene Vogel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 57. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thür, Thier, thun/thust, Rath, Noth, todt und Thränen).
about: A quest tale (KHM 57) built on threes: three sons, three golden things to steal, and a warning before each theft that the hero hears and disregards. What holds it together is the fox, who advises, carries and rescues, and who asks at last for a payment the young man cannot bring himself to make until much later. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as Rath, Thier, thun, gieng, fieng, Wirthshaus and todt.

sentences.t: Es war vor Zeiten ein König, der hatte einen schönen Lustgarten hinter seinem Schloß, darin stand ein Baum, der goldene Äpfel trug.
sentences.l: There was in times past a king, who had a beautiful pleasure-garden behind his castle; in it stood a tree that bore golden apples.
sentences.i: In times gone by there was a king who had a fine pleasure garden behind his castle, and in it stood a tree that bore golden apples.
sentences.n: “vor Zeiten” = in times past, a plainer opening than the usual “es war einmal”. The clauses are simply strung together with der… darin…, the loose, spoken rhythm the tales keep throughout.

sentences.t: Als die Äpfel reiften, wurden sie gezählt, aber gleich den nächsten Morgen fehlte einer.
sentences.l: When the apples ripened, they were counted, but right the next morning one was missing.
sentences.n: “den nächsten Morgen” is a bare accusative of time — no preposition, where English needs an “on”. einer stands alone for one of them.

sentences.t: Das ward dem König gemeldet, und er befahl daß alle Nächte unter dem Baume Wache sollte gehalten werden.
sentences.l: That was reported to the king, and he ordered that every night watch should be kept under the tree.
sentences.i: This was reported to the king, and he gave orders that watch be kept under the tree every night.
sentences.n: “Wache halten” = to keep watch; “alle Nächte” = every night. The passive infinitive waits at the very end, after the modal: “sollte gehalten werden”.

sentences.t: Der König hatte drei Söhne, davon schickte er den ältesten bei einbrechender Nacht in den Garten: wie es aber Mitternacht war, konnte er sich des Schlafes nicht erwehren, und am nächsten Morgen fehlte wieder ein Apfel.
sentences.l: The king had three sons; of them he sent the eldest into the garden at falling night: but when it was midnight, he could not fend off sleep, and the next morning an apple was missing again.
sentences.i: The king had three sons, and of these he sent the eldest into the garden at nightfall; but when midnight came he could not keep sleep off, and the next morning an apple was missing again.
sentences.n: “bei einbrechender Nacht” — literally “at breaking-in night”, i.e. at nightfall. “sich einer Sache erwehren” (to fend a thing off) takes the genitive: “des Schlafes”.

sentences.t: In der folgenden Nacht mußte der zweite Sohn wachen, aber dem ergieng es nicht besser: als es zwölf Uhr geschlagen hatte, schlief er ein, und Morgens fehlte ein Apfel.
sentences.l: In the following night the second son had to keep watch, but to that one it went no better: when it had struck twelve o’clock, he fell asleep, and in the morning an apple was missing.
sentences.i: The next night the second son had to keep watch, but he fared no better: when the clock had struck twelve he fell asleep, and in the morning an apple was gone.
sentences.n: “es ergieng ihm nicht besser” — the impersonal ergehen with a dative: he fared no better. dem is a pointing demonstrative, “that one”. Morgens = of a morning, in the morning.

sentences.t: Jetzt kam die Reihe zu wachen an den dritten Sohn, der war auch bereit, aber der König traute ihm nicht viel zu und meinte er würde noch weniger ausrichten als seine Brüder: endlich aber gestattete er es doch.
sentences.l: Now came the turn to keep watch to the third son; he was ready too, but the king did not credit him with much and thought he would accomplish still less than his brothers: at last, however, he permitted it after all.
sentences.i: Now the turn to keep watch came to the third son, and he was ready enough; but the king did not think much of him and supposed he would accomplish even less than his brothers — yet in the end he permitted it.
sentences.n: “jemandem etwas zutrauen” = to credit someone with being able to do a thing. ausrichten here = to get done, accomplish.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling legte sich also unter den Baum, wachte und ließ den Schlaf nicht Herr werden.
sentences.l: The youth therefore laid himself under the tree, kept watch and did not let sleep become master.
sentences.i: So the youth lay down under the tree, kept watch, and did not let sleep get the mastery of him.
sentences.n: “Herr werden” = to become master — the German makes sleep the would-be lord.

sentences.t: Als es zwölf schlug, so rauschte etwas durch die Luft, und er sah im Mondschein einen Vogel daher fliegen, dessen Gefieder ganz von Gold glänzte.
sentences.l: When it struck twelve, something rushed through the air, and he saw in the moonlight a bird come flying along, whose plumage shone entirely of gold.
sentences.i: As the clock struck twelve, something came rushing through the air, and by moonlight he saw a bird come flying towards him, its plumage all shining gold.
sentences.n: rauschen is the sound of rushing air or water. daherfliegen = to come flying along, towards the watcher.

sentences.t: Der Vogel ließ sich auf dem Baume nieder und hatte eben einen Apfel abgepickt, als der Jüngling einen Pfeil nach ihm abschoß.
sentences.l: The bird let itself down on the tree and had just picked off an apple, when the youth shot an arrow off at him.
sentences.i: The bird settled on the tree and had just pecked off an apple when the youth loosed an arrow at him.
sentences.n: “sich niederlassen” = to alight, settle — reflexive and separable. eben here = just now.

sentences.t: Der Vogel entflog, aber der Pfeil hatte sein Gefieder getroffen, und eine seiner goldenen Federn fiel herab.
sentences.l: The bird flew off, but the arrow had struck his plumage, and one of his golden feathers fell down.
sentences.n: ent- carries the sense of away, off — entfliegen, to fly off, and likewise entkommen, entlaufen. “eine seiner Federn” is a partitive genitive: one of his feathers.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling hob sie auf, brachte sie am andern Morgen dem König und erzählte ihm was er in der Nacht gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: The youth picked it up, brought it to the king the next morning and told him what he had seen in the night.
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” = the next morning — ander here means “next”, not “other”; the phrase returns again and again in this tale.

sentences.t: Der König versammelte seinen Rath, und jedermann erklärte eine Feder wie diese sei mehr werth als das gesammte Königreich.
sentences.l: The king assembled his council, and everyone declared a feather like this one was worth more than the entire kingdom.
sentences.i: The king summoned his council, and every man of them declared that a single feather like this was worth more than the whole kingdom.
sentences.n: Rath does double duty: advice, and the body that gives it — here the council. sei is the subjunctive of reported speech. gesammte = modern gesamte, werth = wert.

sentences.t: „Ist die Feder so kostbar,“ erklärte der König, „so hilft mir auch die eine nichts, sondern ich will und muß den ganzen Vogel haben.“
sentences.l: “Is the feather so precious,” declared the king, “then the one alone helps me nothing either, but rather I will and must have the whole bird.”
sentences.i: “If the feather is so precious,” declared the king, “then the one is no use to me: I will and must have the whole bird.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: putting the verb first (“Ist die Feder…”) is German’s way of saying “if the feather is…”, and so answers it.

sentences.t: Der älteste Sohn machte sich auf den Weg, verließ sich auf seine Klugheit und meinte den goldenen Vogel schon zu finden.
sentences.l: The eldest son set himself on the way, relied on his cleverness and thought to find the golden bird easily enough.
sentences.i: The eldest son set out, trusted to his own cleverness, and supposed he would find the golden bird readily enough.
sentences.n: “sich auf den Weg machen” = to set out. “sich verlassen auf” = to rely on — a different verb from verlassen, to forsake. schon here is the confident “surely, easily enough”.

sentences.t: Wie er eine Strecke gegangen war, sah er an dem Rande eines Waldes einen Fuchs sitzen, legte seine Flinte an und zielte auf ihn.
sentences.l: When he had gone a stretch, he saw at the edge of a forest a fox sitting, laid his gun on and aimed at him.
sentences.i: When he had gone some way he saw a fox sitting at the edge of a wood; he levelled his gun and took aim at him.
sentences.n: “anlegen” of a gun = to bring it up, to level it. wie here = when, as often in these tales.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs rief „schieß mich nicht, ich will dir dafür einen guten Rath geben.
sentences.l: The fox called “do not shoot me, I will give you a good piece of counsel for it.
sentences.i: The fox called out: “Don’t shoot me — I will give you a good piece of advice in return.
sentences.n: Rath (modern Rat) here is advice; dafür = for that, in return.

sentences.t: Du bist auf dem Weg nach dem goldenen Vogel, und wirst heut Abend in ein Dorf kommen, wo zwei Wirthshäuser einander gegenüber stehen.
sentences.l: You are on the way after the golden bird, and will come this evening into a village where two inns stand opposite one another.
sentences.i: You are on your way to the golden bird, and this evening you will come to a village where two inns stand facing each other.
sentences.n: Wirthshaus = modern Wirtshaus, an inn; heut = heute.

sentences.t: Eins ist hell erleuchtet, und es geht darin lustig her: da kehr aber nicht ein, sondern geh ins andere, wenn es dich auch schlecht ansieht.“
sentences.l: One is brightly lit, and it goes merrily in it: but do not turn in there, but rather go into the other, even if it looks poorly at you.”
sentences.i: One is brightly lit, and things are lively inside; but do not put up there — go into the other, even if it makes a poor showing.”
sentences.n: “es geht lustig her” = things are lively there. “einkehren” = to stop and put up at an inn. “wenn es dich auch schlecht ansieht” — literally “even if it looks at you badly”, i.e. even if it seems unwelcoming.

sentences.t: „Wie kann mir wohl so ein albernes Thier einen vernünftigen Rath ertheilen!“ dachte der Königssohn und drückte los, aber er fehlte den Fuchs, der den Schwanz streckte und schnell in den Wald lief.
sentences.l: “How can such a silly animal give me sensible counsel!” thought the king’s son, and pulled the trigger, but he missed the fox, who stretched out his tail and ran quickly into the forest.
sentences.i: “How should so silly a beast give me sensible advice!” thought the king’s son, and fired — but he missed the fox, who stretched out his tail and ran off quickly into the wood.
sentences.n: Thier = modern Tier. “losdrücken” = to pull the trigger. fehlen is transitive here: to miss a target.

sentences.t: Darauf setzte er seinen Weg fort und kam Abends in das Dorf, wo die beiden Wirthshäuser standen: in dem einen ward gesungen und gesprungen, das andere hatte ein armseliges betrübtes Ansehen.
sentences.l: Thereupon he continued his way and came in the evening into the village where the two inns stood: in the one there was singing and leaping, the other had a wretched, dismal look.
sentences.i: Thereupon he went on his way and came in the evening to the village where the two inns stood: in the one there was singing and dancing, while the other had a wretched, gloomy look about it.
sentences.n: “ward gesungen und gesprungen” is an impersonal passive — “there was singing and leaping”, with nobody named as doing it.

sentences.t: „Ich wäre wohl ein Narr,“ dachte er, „wenn ich in das lumpige Wirthshaus gienge und das schöne liegen ließ.“
sentences.l: “I would surely be a fool,” he thought, “if I went into the shabby inn and let the fine one lie.”
sentences.i: “I should be a fool,” he thought, “to go into the shabby inn and let the fine one stand.”
sentences.n: wäre and gienge are subjunctive — an unreal condition. ließ is written without the -e of ließe, so the last verb of the three looks like a plain past. “liegen lassen” = to leave a thing lying, to pass it by.

sentences.t: Also gieng er in das lustige ein, lebte da in Saus und Braus, und vergaß den Vogel seinen Vater und alle guten Lehren.
sentences.l: So he went into the merry one, lived there in rush and roar, and forgot the bird, his father and all good teachings.
sentences.i: So he put up at the merry one, lived there in riot and revelry, and forgot the bird, his father, and all good counsel.
sentences.n: “gieng… ein” is eingehen, to go in — not the fox's einkehren, to put up at an inn, though it comes to the same thing here. “in Saus und Braus leben” is a set phrase for living high and wastefully; both halves come from verbs of rushing noise, sausen and brausen. The list runs on without commas: “den Vogel seinen Vater und alle guten Lehren”.

sentences.t: Als eine Zeit verstrichen und der älteste Sohn immer und immer nicht nach Haus gekommen war, so machte sich der zweite auf den Weg und wollte den goldenen Vogel suchen.
sentences.l: When a time had elapsed and the eldest son had still and still not come home, then the second set himself on the way and wanted to seek the golden bird.
sentences.i: When some time had passed and the eldest son still had not come home, the second set out to look for the golden bird.
sentences.n: “immer und immer nicht” — “still and still not”, an emphatic doubling: he simply never came.

sentences.t: Wie dem ältesten begegnete ihm der Fuchs und gab ihm den guten Rath, den er nicht achtete.
sentences.l: As with the eldest, the fox met him and gave him the good counsel, which he did not heed.
sentences.i: As with the eldest, the fox met him and gave him the good advice, which he did not heed.
sentences.n: begegnen takes a dative — the person met stands in the dative (ihm, dem ältesten), so German says “met to him”.

sentences.t: Er kam zu den beiden Wirthshäusern, wo sein Bruder am Fenster des einen stand, aus dem der Jubel erschallte, und ihn anrief.
sentences.l: He came to the two inns, where his brother stood at the window of the one out of which the rejoicing rang, and called to him.
sentences.i: He came to the two inns, where his brother stood at the window of the one from which the merrymaking rang out, and called to him.
sentences.n: “des einen” is a genitive with its noun left out — of the one inn — and that inn is taken up again by “aus dem”, out of which. Wirthshaus = modern Wirtshaus.

sentences.t: Er konnte nicht widerstehen, gieng hinein und lebte nur seinen Lüsten.
sentences.l: He could not resist, went in and lived only to his appetites.
sentences.i: He could not resist; he went in and lived for nothing but his pleasures.
sentences.n: “seinen Lüsten leben” — to live to one’s desires; the dative names what the living is given over to.

sentences.t: Wiederum verstrich eine Zeit, da wollte der jüngste Königssohn ausziehen und sein Heil versuchen, der Vater aber wollte es nicht zulassen.
sentences.l: Again a time elapsed; then the youngest king’s son wanted to set out and try his fortune, but the father would not permit it.
sentences.i: Again some time passed, and then the youngest king’s son wished to set out and try his luck; but the father would not permit it.
sentences.n: “sein Heil versuchen” = to try one’s fortune (Heil = welfare, salvation, good luck).

sentences.t: „Es ist vergeblich,“ sprach er, „der wird den goldenen Vogel noch weniger finden als seine Brüder, und wenn ihm ein Unglück zustößt, so weiß er sich nicht zu helfen; es fehlt ihm am Besten.“
sentences.l: “It is in vain,” he spoke, “that one will find the golden bird still less than his brothers, and if a misfortune befalls him, then he does not know how to help himself; the best is wanting in him.”
sentences.i: “It is useless,” he said. “He will find the golden bird even less than his brothers did; and if some misfortune befalls him he will not know how to help himself — he has not what it takes.”
sentences.n: “es fehlt ihm am Besten” — literally “the best is lacking in him”: he wants the very thing that matters, sense and capability. “zustoßen” is used of misfortunes befalling a person, who stands in the dative.

sentences.t: Doch endlich, wie keine Ruhe mehr da war, ließ er ihn ziehen.
sentences.l: Yet at last, when there was no peace any more, he let him go.
sentences.i: Yet in the end, when there was no more peace to be had, he let him go.
sentences.n: ziehen here = to travel, to go one’s way, as in ausziehen just above.

sentences.t: Vor dem Walde saß wieder der Fuchs, bat um sein Leben und ertheilte den guten Rath.
sentences.l: Before the forest sat the fox again, begged for his life and gave the good counsel.
sentences.i: Before the wood the fox sat again, begged for his life, and gave the good advice.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling war gutmüthig und sagte „sei ruhig, Füchslein, ich thue dir nichts zu Leid.“
sentences.l: The youth was good-natured and said “be easy, little-fox, I do you nothing to harm.”
sentences.i: The youth was good-natured and said: “Be easy, little fox, I shall do you no harm.”
sentences.n: “jemandem etwas zu Leid thun” = to do someone a harm (modern zuleide tun). Füchslein is the diminutive, “little fox”; gutmüthig = modern gutmütig.

sentences.t: „Es soll dich nicht gereuen,“ antwortete der Fuchs, „und damit du schneller fortkommst, so steig hinten auf meinen Schwanz.“
sentences.l: “It shall not rue you,” answered the fox, “and so that you get on faster, climb up behind onto my tail.”
sentences.i: “You shall not regret it,” answered the fox, “and so that you may get on faster, climb up behind on my tail.”
sentences.n: “es gereut mich” is an old impersonal turn — “it causes me regret”; the person is the object, not the subject. “fortkommen” = to make headway.

sentences.t: Und kaum hat er sich aufgesetzt, so fieng der Fuchs an zu laufen, und da giengs über Stock und Stein daß die Haare im Winde pfiffen.
sentences.l: And scarcely has he seated himself up, then the fox began to run, and there it went over stick and stone so that the hairs whistled in the wind.
sentences.i: And scarcely had he seated himself when the fox began to run, and off they went over stock and stone, so that his hair whistled in the wind.
sentences.n: “kaum… so…” = no sooner… than. The present hat inside a past narrative is the storyteller’s vivid present. “über Stock und Stein” = over stick and stone, headlong across rough country — the flourish returns at each of the fox's rides, the wording shifted a little each time.

sentences.t: Als sie zu dem Dorfe kamen, stieg der Jüngling ab, befolgte den guten Rath und kehrte, ohne sich umzusehen, in das geringe Wirthshaus ein, wo er ruhig übernachtete.
sentences.l: When they came to the village, the youth climbed down, followed the good counsel and turned in, without looking about him, at the poor inn, where he spent the night quietly.
sentences.i: When they came to the village the youth got down, followed the good advice, and turned in — without so much as a glance about him — at the humble inn, where he passed a quiet night.
sentences.n: einkehren is separable, and here the whole phrase “ohne sich umzusehen” sits inside the split verb: “kehrte… ein”. gering = modest, of little account.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen, wie er auf das Feld kam, saß da schon der Fuchs und sagte „ich will dir weiter sagen was du zu thun hast.
sentences.l: The next morning, when he came out onto the field, the fox already sat there and said “I will tell you further what you have to do.
sentences.i: The next morning, when he came out into the field, the fox was already sitting there, and said: “I will tell you further what you are to do.
sentences.n: “zu thun haben” (modern zu tun haben): haben + zu + infinitive states an obligation, what one has to do.

sentences.t: Geh du immer gerade aus, endlich wirst du an ein Schloß kommen, vor dem eine ganze Schaar Soldaten liegt, aber kümmre dich nicht darum, denn sie werden alle schlafen und schnarchen:
sentences.l: Go you ever straight ahead, at last you will come to a castle, before which a whole troop of soldiers lies, but do not trouble yourself about them, for they will all be sleeping and snoring:
sentences.i: Keep straight on, and at last you will come to a castle with a whole company of soldiers lying before it; but pay no heed to them, for they will all be asleep and snoring.
sentences.n: “geradeaus gehen” = to keep straight on; the du after the imperative is emphatic. “sich kümmern um” = to concern oneself with. Schaar = modern Schar, a troop.

sentences.t: geh mitten durch und geradeswegs in das Schloß hinein, und geh durch alle Stuben, zuletzt wirst du in eine Kammer kommen, wo ein goldener Vogel in einem hölzernen Käfig hängt.
sentences.l: go right through the middle and straightway into the castle, and go through all the rooms; at last you will come into a chamber where a golden bird hangs in a wooden cage.
sentences.i: Go right through the midst of them and straight into the castle, and pass through all the rooms; at the last you will come to a chamber where a golden bird hangs in a wooden cage.
sentences.n: geradeswegs = straightway, by the direct road — an old genitive frozen into an adverb.

sentences.t: Neben an steht ein leerer Goldkäfig zum Prunk, aber hüte dich daß du den Vogel nicht aus seinem schlechten Käfig heraus nimmst und in den prächtigen thust, sonst möchte es dir schlimm ergehen.“
sentences.l: Next to it stands an empty gold-cage for show, but guard yourself that you do not take the bird out of his poor cage and put him into the splendid one, else it might go badly for you.”
sentences.i: Beside it stands an empty golden cage, for show; but take care not to lift the bird out of his poor cage and put him into the splendid one, or it may go badly with you.”
sentences.n: “sich hüten daß” = to take care that (not). “zum Prunk” = for display. thust = modern tust. “es ergeht dir schlimm” — the impersonal ergehen again: things go badly for you. The warning comes back twice more, the modal changing each time: möchte here, then wird, then kann.

sentences.t: Nach diesen Worten streckte der Fuchs wieder seinen Schwanz aus, und der Königssohn setzte sich auf: da giengs über Stock und Stein daß die Haare im Winde pfiffen.
sentences.l: After these words the fox stretched out his tail again, and the king’s son seated himself up: then it went over stick and stone so that the hairs whistled in the wind.
sentences.i: After these words the fox stretched out his tail again, and the king’s son mounted; and off they went over stock and stone, so that his hair whistled in the wind.

sentences.t: Als er bei dem Schloß angelangt war, fand er alles so wie der Fuchs gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: When he had arrived at the castle, he found everything just as the fox had said.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn kam in die Kammer, wo der goldene Vogel in einem hölzernen Käfig saß, und ein goldener stand daneben: die drei goldenen Äpfel aber lagen in der Stube umher.
sentences.l: The king’s son came into the chamber where the golden bird sat in a wooden cage, and a golden one stood beside it: but the three golden apples lay about in the room.
sentences.i: The king’s son came into the chamber where the golden bird sat in a wooden cage, with a golden one standing beside it; and the three golden apples lay scattered about the room.
sentences.n: “ein goldener” — the adjective stands alone for “a golden one”, with no noun repeated. The stolen apples are lying there: the only word the tale spends on where they went.

sentences.t: Da dachte er es wäre lächerlich, wenn er den schönen Vogel in dem gemeinen und häßlichen Käfig lassen wollte, öffnete die Thüre, packte ihn und setzte ihn in den goldenen.
sentences.l: Then he thought it would be laughable if he wanted to leave the beautiful bird in the common and ugly cage, opened the door, seized him and set him in the golden one.
sentences.i: Then he thought it would be absurd to leave so beautiful a bird in the common, ugly cage; he opened the door, took hold of him, and set him in the golden one.
sentences.n: gemein here means common, ordinary — not “mean”. wäre is the subjunctive of the thought he entertains; Thüre = modern Tür.

sentences.t: In dem Augenblick aber that der Vogel einen durchdringenden Schrei.
sentences.l: In that moment, however, the bird did a piercing cry.
sentences.i: But in that instant the bird gave a piercing shriek.
sentences.n: “einen Schrei thun” — German “does” a cry where English gives one; that = modern tat.

sentences.t: Die Soldaten erwachten, stürzten herein und führten ihn ins Gefängnis.
sentences.l: The soldiers awoke, rushed in and led him into the prison.
sentences.i: The soldiers awoke, came rushing in, and took him off to prison.

sentences.t: Den andern Morgen wurde er vor ein Gericht gestellt und, da er alles bekannte, zum Tode verurtheilt.
sentences.l: The next morning he was set before a court and, since he confessed everything, condemned to death.
sentences.i: The next morning he was brought before a court and, since he confessed everything, condemned to death.
sentences.n: “den andern Morgen” is a bare accusative of time, “on the next morning”. verurtheilt = modern verurteilt.

sentences.t: Doch sagte der König er wollte ihm unter einer Bedingung das Leben schenken, wenn er ihm nämlich das goldene Pferd brächte, welches noch schneller liefe als der Wind, und dann sollte er obendrein zur Belohnung den goldenen Vogel erhalten.
sentences.l: Yet the king said he would grant him his life on one condition, namely if he brought him the golden horse, which ran still faster than the wind, and then he should receive the golden bird into the bargain as a reward.
sentences.i: Yet the king said he would spare his life on one condition: that he bring him the golden horse, which runs faster than the wind; and then he should have the golden bird as a reward besides.
sentences.n: “das Leben schenken” = to make a gift of a life, i.e. to spare it. wollte, brächte, liefe are all subjunctive — the king’s words as reported. obendrein = on top of that.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn machte sich auf den Weg, seufzte aber und war traurig, denn wo sollte er das goldene Pferd finden?
sentences.l: The king’s son set himself on the way, but sighed and was sad, for where should he find the golden horse?
sentences.i: The king’s son set out, but he sighed and was downcast — for where was he to find the golden horse?
sentences.n: The question is the young man’s own thought, dropped into the narration without any “he wondered”.

sentences.t: Da sah er auf einmal seinen alten Freund, den Fuchs, an dem Wege sitzen.
sentences.l: Then he saw all at once his old friend, the fox, sitting by the way.
sentences.i: Then all at once he saw his old friend the fox sitting by the roadside.
sentences.n: sehen takes an object and a bare infinitive — “sah … den Fuchs … sitzen”, saw the fox sit, with no “to” and no participle. The old dative -e survives in “an dem Wege”.

sentences.t: „Siehst du,“ sprach der Fuchs, „so ist es gekommen, weil du mir nicht gehört hast.
sentences.l: “You see,” spoke the fox, “so it has come about, because you did not listen to me.
sentences.i: “There, you see,” said the fox, “this is what has come of it, because you did not listen to me.
sentences.n: hören with a dative (mir) = to listen to, to obey someone.

sentences.t: Doch sei gutes Muthes, ich will mich deiner annehmen und dir sagen wie du zu dem goldenen Pferd gelangst.
sentences.l: Yet be of good courage, I will take charge of you and tell you how you get to the golden horse.
sentences.i: But be of good heart: I will take you in hand and tell you how to come by the golden horse.
sentences.n: “sei gutes Muthes” — a genitive of quality, “be of good courage” (Muth = modern Mut). “sich jemandes annehmen” = to take someone’s part, to look after them; it too takes the genitive, deiner.

sentences.t: Du mußt gerades Weges fortgehen, so wirst du zu einem Schloß kommen, wo das Pferd im Stalle steht.
sentences.l: You must go on by the straight way, then you will come to a castle where the horse stands in the stable.
sentences.i: You must go straight on, and you will come to a castle where the horse stands in the stable.
sentences.n: “gerades Weges” — another frozen genitive: by the direct road.

sentences.t: Vor dem Stall werden die Stallknechte liegen, aber sie werden schlafen und schnarchen, und du kannst geruhig das goldene Pferd herausführen.
sentences.l: Before the stable the stable-hands will be lying, but they will be sleeping and snoring, and you can calmly lead the golden horse out.
sentences.i: The grooms will be lying before the stable, but they will be asleep and snoring, and you may lead the golden horse out at your leisure.
sentences.n: geruhig = modern ruhig, calmly, undisturbed.

sentences.t: Aber eins mußt du in acht nehmen, leg ihm den schlechten Sattel von Holz und Leder auf und ja nicht den goldenen, der dabei hängt, sonst wird es dir schlimm ergehen.“
sentences.l: But one thing you must take in heed: lay the poor saddle of wood and leather on him and by no means the golden one that hangs beside it, else it will go badly for you.”
sentences.i: But one thing you must take care of: lay the poor saddle of wood and leather on him, and on no account the golden one hanging beside it, or it will go badly with you.”
sentences.n: “in acht nehmen” = to take heed of. ja with a negative is emphatic: on no account. “auflegen” is separable — “leg… auf”.

sentences.t: Dann streckte der Fuchs seinen Schwanz aus, der Königssohn setzte sich auf, und es gieng fort über Stock und Stein daß die Haare im Winde pfiffen.
sentences.l: Then the fox stretched out his tail, the king’s son seated himself up, and away it went over stick and stone so that the hairs whistled in the wind.
sentences.i: Then the fox stretched out his tail, the king’s son mounted, and away they went over stock and stone, so that his hair whistled in the wind.

sentences.t: Alles traf so ein, wie der Fuchs gesagt hatte, er kam in den Stall, wo das goldene Pferd stand:
sentences.l: Everything came about just as the fox had said; he came into the stable where the golden horse stood:
sentences.i: Everything fell out just as the fox had said. He came into the stable where the golden horse stood.
sentences.n: “eintreffen” of a prediction = to come true, to come to pass.

sentences.t: als er ihm aber den schlechten Sattel auflegen wollte, so dachte er „ein so schönes Thier wird verschändet, wenn ich ihm nicht den guten Sattel auflege, der ihm gebührt.“
sentences.l: but when he wanted to lay the poor saddle on him, he thought “so beautiful an animal is disgraced if I do not lay on him the good saddle that is due to him.”
sentences.i: But when he was about to put the poor saddle on him, he thought: “So fine a beast is shamed if I do not give him the good saddle that is his due.”
sentences.n: verschänden (to disfigure, dishonour) is a rare old word, close to schänden, to defile. gebühren with a dative = to be due to someone.

sentences.t: Kaum aber berührte der goldene Sattel das Pferd, so fieng es an laut zu wiehern.
sentences.l: But scarcely did the golden saddle touch the horse, then it began to neigh loudly.
sentences.i: But scarcely had the golden saddle touched the horse when it began to neigh aloud.
sentences.n: The “kaum …, so …” pair again — modern German answers kaum with als.

sentences.t: Die Stallknechte erwachten, ergriffen den Jüngling und warfen ihn ins Gefängnis.
sentences.l: The stable-hands awoke, seized the youth and threw him into the prison.
sentences.i: The grooms awoke, seized the youth, and threw him into prison.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen wurde er vom Gerichte zum Tode verurtheilt, doch versprach ihm der König das Leben zu schenken und dazu das goldene Pferd, wenn er die schöne Königstochter vom goldenen Schlosse herbeischaffen könnte.
sentences.l: The next morning he was condemned to death by the court, yet the king promised to grant him his life and the golden horse with it, if he could bring the beautiful king’s-daughter from the golden castle here.
sentences.i: The next morning he was condemned to death by the court; yet the king promised to spare his life, and to give him the golden horse into the bargain, if he could fetch the beautiful king’s daughter from the golden castle.
sentences.n: “herbeischaffen” = to bring here, to procure. könnte is the subjunctive inside the king’s reported promise. The tale’s pattern is now set: each theft fails, and each failure buys a harder errand.

sentences.t: Mit schwerem Herzen machte sich der Jüngling auf den Weg, doch zu seinem Glücke fand er bald den treuen Fuchs.
sentences.l: With heavy heart the youth set himself on the way, yet to his fortune he soon found the faithful fox.
sentences.i: With a heavy heart the youth set out; yet by his good fortune he soon found the faithful fox.

sentences.t: „Ich sollte dich nur deinem Unglück überlassen,“ sagte der Fuchs, „aber ich habe Mitleiden mit dir und will dir noch einmal aus deiner Noth helfen.
sentences.l: “I ought just to leave you to your misfortune,” said the fox, “but I have compassion with you and will help you out of your need once more.
sentences.i: “I ought to leave you to your misfortune,” said the fox, “but I pity you, and I will help you out of your trouble once again.
sentences.n: Mitleiden (modern Mitleid) = compassion, literally “suffering-with”. Noth = modern Not, distress.

sentences.t: Dein Weg führt dich gerade zu dem goldenen Schlosse: Abends wirst du anlangen, und Nachts, wenn alles still ist, dann geht die schöne Königstochter ins Badehaus, um da zu baden.
sentences.l: Your way leads you straight to the golden castle: in the evening you will arrive, and at night, when everything is still, then the beautiful king’s daughter goes into the bath-house, to bathe there.
sentences.i: Your road leads you straight to the golden castle. You will arrive in the evening; and at night, when all is still, the beautiful king’s daughter goes to the bath-house to bathe.
sentences.n: Abends and Nachts are old adverbial genitives — of an evening, of a night, meaning as a rule at that time. “um… zu” = in order to.

sentences.t: Und wenn sie hineingeht, so spring auf sie zu und gib ihr einen Kuß, dann folgt sie dir, und du kannst sie mit dir fortführen:
sentences.l: And when she goes in, then spring up to her and give her a kiss, then she follows you, and you can lead her away with you:
sentences.i: And when she goes in, spring up to her and give her a kiss; then she will follow you, and you may carry her off with you.
sentences.n: “auf jemanden zuspringen” — the zu of direction goes to the end: “spring auf sie zu”.

sentences.t: nur dulde nicht daß sie vorher von ihren Eltern Abschied nimmt, sonst kann es dir schlimm ergehen.“
sentences.l: only do not suffer that she takes leave of her parents beforehand, else it can go badly for you.”
sentences.i: Only do not allow her to take leave of her parents first, or it may go badly with you.”
sentences.n: “Abschied nehmen von” = to take leave of. dulden = to tolerate, to allow.

sentences.t: Dann streckte der Fuchs seinen Schwanz, der Königssohn setzte sich auf, und so gieng es über Stock und Stein daß die Haare im Winde pfiffen.
sentences.l: Then the fox stretched out his tail, the king’s son seated himself up, and so it went over stick and stone so that the hairs whistled in the wind.
sentences.i: Then the fox stretched out his tail, the king’s son mounted, and so they went over stock and stone, with his hair whistling in the wind.

sentences.t: Als er beim goldenen Schloß ankam, war es so wie der Fuchs gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: When he arrived at the golden castle, it was just as the fox had said.

sentences.t: Er wartete bis um Mitternacht, als alles in tiefem Schlaf lag, und die schöne Jungfrau ins Badehaus gieng, da sprang er hervor und gab ihr einen Kuß.
sentences.l: He waited until about midnight, when everything lay in deep sleep and the beautiful maiden went into the bath-house; then he sprang forth and gave her a kiss.
sentences.i: He waited till about midnight, when all lay in deep sleep and the beautiful maiden went to the bath-house; then he sprang out and gave her a kiss.

sentences.t: Sie sagte sie wollte gerne mit ihm gehen, bat ihn aber flehentlich und mit Thränen er möchte ihr erlauben vorher von ihren Eltern Abschied zu nehmen.
sentences.l: She said she would gladly go with him, but begged him imploringly and with tears he might allow her to take leave of her parents beforehand.
sentences.i: She said she would gladly go with him, but begged him imploringly and in tears that he would let her take leave of her parents first.
sentences.n: wollte and möchte are subjunctives of reported speech — her words as he heard them. Thränen = modern Tränen.

sentences.t: Er widerstand anfänglich ihren Bitten, als sie aber immer mehr weinte und ihm zu Fuß fiel, so gab er endlich nach.
sentences.l: He withstood her entreaties at first, but when she wept more and more and fell at his foot, then he at last gave in.
sentences.i: At first he withstood her entreaties; but when she wept more and more and fell at his feet, he gave in at last.
sentences.n: “zu Fuß fallen” — to fall at someone’s feet, singular Fuß in the old phrase. “nachgeben” = to give in.

sentences.t: Kaum aber war die Jungfrau zu dem Bette ihres Vaters getreten, so wachte er und alle anderen, die im Schloß waren, auf, und der Jüngling ward fest gehalten und ins Gefängnis gesetzt.
sentences.l: But scarcely had the maiden stepped to her father’s bed, then he and all the others who were in the castle woke up, and the youth was held fast and set into prison.
sentences.i: But scarcely had the maiden come to her father’s bed when he woke, and all the others in the castle with him; and the youth was seized and put in prison.
sentences.n: “aufwachen” is separable, and here the auf waits out a whole relative clause before it lands: “so wachte er und alle anderen, die im Schloß waren, auf”.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen sprach der König zu ihm „dein Leben ist verwirkt, und du kannst bloß Gnade finden wenn du den Berg abträgst, der vor meinen Fenstern liegt, und über welchen ich nicht hinaus sehen kann, und das mußt du binnen acht Tagen zu Stande bringen.
sentences.l: The next morning the king spoke to him “your life is forfeit, and you can find mercy only if you carry off the mountain that lies before my windows, and over which I cannot see out, and that you must bring to accomplishment within eight days.
sentences.i: The next morning the king said to him: “Your life is forfeit, and you can find mercy only if you carry away the mountain that lies before my windows and shuts off my view — and that you must bring about within eight days.
sentences.n: verwirkt = forfeited. “abtragen” = to carry off, to level. “zu Stande bringen” = to bring about (modern zustande). “binnen acht Tagen” = within eight days.

sentences.t: Gelingt dir das, so sollst du meine Tochter zur Belohnung haben.“
sentences.l: Succeeds that for you, then you shall have my daughter as reward.”
sentences.i: If you succeed in it, you shall have my daughter for your reward.”
sentences.n: Another verb-first conditional: “Gelingt dir das” = if that succeeds for you. gelingen takes a dative of the person — the thing succeeds to you.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn fieng an, grub und schaufelte ohne abzulassen, als er aber nach sieben Tagen sah wie wenig er ausgerichtet hatte, und alle seine Arbeit so gut wie nichts war, so fiel er in große Traurigkeit und gab alle Hoffnung auf.
sentences.l: The king’s son began, dug and shovelled without leaving off; but when after seven days he saw how little he had accomplished, and all his work was as good as nothing, then he fell into great sadness and gave up all hope.
sentences.i: The king’s son set to; he dug and shovelled without ceasing. But when after seven days he saw how little he had accomplished, and that all his labour came to as good as nothing, he fell into deep sorrow and gave up all hope.
sentences.n: “ablassen” = to leave off; in “ohne abzulassen” the zu sits inside the separable verb, ab-zu-lassen.

sentences.t: Am Abend des siebenten Tags aber erschien der Fuchs und sagte „du verdienst nicht daß ich mich deiner annehme, aber geh nur hin und lege dich schlafen, ich will die Arbeit für dich thun.“
sentences.l: But on the evening of the seventh day the fox appeared and said “you do not deserve that I should take charge of you, but just go along and lay yourself down to sleep, I will do the work for you.”
sentences.i: But on the evening of the seventh day the fox appeared and said: “You do not deserve that I should take your part; but go along and lie down to sleep — I will do the work for you.”
sentences.n: annehme is subjunctive after “du verdienst nicht daß…”. nur is the softening “just”, as in “geh nur hin”.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen als er erwachte und zum Fenster hinaus sah, so war der Berg verschwunden.
sentences.l: The next morning when he awoke and looked out at the window, the mountain had vanished.
sentences.i: The next morning, when he awoke and looked out of the window, the mountain had vanished.
sentences.n: “zum Fenster hinaus sehen” — to look out at the window, the German tracing the way the gaze travels.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling eilte voll Freude zum König und meldete ihm daß die Bedingung erfüllt wäre, und der König mochte wollen oder nicht, er mußte Wort halten und ihm seine Tochter geben.
sentences.l: The youth hurried full of joy to the king and reported to him that the condition was fulfilled, and the king might want to or not, he had to keep word and give him his daughter.
sentences.i: Full of joy the youth hurried to the king and told him the condition was fulfilled; and whether the king liked it or not, he had to keep his word and give him his daughter.
sentences.n: “der König mochte wollen oder nicht” — “the king might will or not”, i.e. like it or not. “Wort halten” = to keep one’s word. wäre is again the subjunctive of what is reported.

sentences.t: Nun zogen die beiden zusammen fort, und es währte nicht lange, so kam der treue Fuchs zu ihnen.
sentences.l: Now the two went away together, and it did not last long, then the faithful fox came to them.
sentences.i: Now the two set off together, and it was not long before the faithful fox came to them.
sentences.n: “es währte nicht lange, so…” = it was not long before…

sentences.t: „Das beste hast du zwar,“ sagte er, „aber zu der Jungfrau aus dem goldenen Schloß gehört auch das goldene Pferd.“
sentences.l: “The best you have indeed,” he said, “but to the maiden from the golden castle belongs the golden horse too.”
sentences.i: “You have the best of it, to be sure,” he said, “but the golden horse belongs with the maiden from the golden castle.”
sentences.n: “gehören zu” = to belong with, to go together with. “zwar… aber” = indeed… but.

sentences.t: „Wie soll ich das bekommen?“ fragte der Jüngling.
sentences.l: “How am I to get that?” asked the youth.

sentences.t: „Das will ich dir sagen,“ antwortete der Fuchs, „zuerst bring dem Könige, der dich nach dem goldenen Schlosse geschickt hat, die schöne Jungfrau.
sentences.l: “That I will tell you,” answered the fox, “first bring the beautiful maiden to the king who sent you to the golden castle.
sentences.n: Könige and Schlosse carry the old dative -e, still usual in 1857 and now dropped.

sentences.t: Da wird unerhörte Freude sein, sie werden dir das goldene Pferd gerne geben und werden dirs vorführen.
sentences.l: There will be unheard-of joy, they will gladly give you the golden horse and will lead it out to you.
sentences.i: There will be unheard-of rejoicing; they will gladly give you the golden horse and will lead it out to you.
sentences.n: “vorführen” = to lead out and present. dirs = dir es.

sentences.t: Setz dich alsbald auf und reiche allen zum Abschied die Hand herab, zuletzt der schönen Jungfrau, und wenn du sie gefaßt hast, so zieh sie mit einem Schwung hinauf und jage davon:
sentences.l: Seat yourself up at once and reach down your hand to all in farewell, last of all to the beautiful maiden, and when you have taken hold of her, then pull her up with one swing and gallop away:
sentences.i: Mount at once, and reach your hand down to them all in farewell, the beautiful maiden last of all; and when you have hold of her, swing her up and gallop away.
sentences.n: The herab in “die Hand herab reichen” marks the direction: down from the saddle. “mit einem Schwung” = with a single swing. “davonjagen” = to tear away.

sentences.t: und niemand ist im Stande dich einzuholen, denn das Pferd läuft schneller als der Wind.“
sentences.l: and nobody is in a state to catch you up, for the horse runs faster than the wind.”
sentences.i: and nobody will be able to overtake you, for the horse runs faster than the wind.”
sentences.n: “im Stande sein” (modern imstande) = to be able. “einholen” = to catch up with; the zu sits inside it, ein-zu-holen.

sentences.t: Alles wurde glücklich vollbracht, und der Königssohn führte die schöne Jungfrau auf dem goldenen Pferde fort.
sentences.l: Everything was happily accomplished, and the king’s son carried the beautiful maiden away on the golden horse.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs blieb nicht zurück und sprach zu dem Jüngling „jetzt will ich dir auch zu dem goldenen Vogel verhelfen.
sentences.l: The fox did not stay behind and spoke to the youth “now I will help you to the golden bird as well.
sentences.i: The fox did not stay behind, and said to the youth: “Now I will help you to the golden bird as well.
sentences.n: “jemandem zu etwas verhelfen” = to help someone to a thing, to help them get it.

sentences.t: Wenn du nahe bei dem Schlosse bist, wo sich der Vogel befindet, so laß die Jungfrau absitzen, und ich will sie in meine Obhut nehmen.
sentences.l: When you are near the castle where the bird finds itself, then let the maiden dismount, and I will take her into my keeping.
sentences.i: When you are near the castle where the bird is, let the maiden dismount, and I will take her into my keeping.
sentences.n: “sich befinden” = to be, to be situated — literally “to find oneself”. “in Obhut nehmen” = to take into one’s care.

sentences.t: Dann reit mit dem goldenen Pferd in den Schloßhof: bei dem Anblick wird große Freude sein, und sie werden dir den goldenen Vogel herausbringen.
sentences.l: Then ride with the golden horse into the castle-yard: at the sight there will be great joy, and they will bring the golden bird out to you.
sentences.i: Then ride the golden horse into the castle yard; at the sight of it there will be great rejoicing, and they will bring the golden bird out to you.

sentences.t: Wie du den Käfig in der Hand hast, so jage zu uns zurück und hole dir die Jungfrau wieder ab.“
sentences.l: As soon as you have the cage in your hand, then gallop back to us and fetch yourself the maiden away again.”
sentences.i: As soon as you have the cage in your hand, gallop back to us and fetch the maiden away again.”
sentences.n: wie here = as soon as. “abholen” = to fetch someone away; dir is a dative of interest — fetch her for yourself.

sentences.t: Als der Anschlag geglückt war und der Königssohn mit seinen Schätzen heim reiten wollte, so sagte der Fuchs „nun sollst du mich für meinen Beistand belohnen.“
sentences.l: When the plan had succeeded and the king’s son wanted to ride home with his treasures, the fox said “now you shall reward me for my assistance.”
sentences.i: When the scheme had succeeded and the king’s son was about to ride home with his treasures, the fox said: “Now you shall reward me for my help.”
sentences.n: Anschlag here is a plan or scheme, not the modern “attack”. Beistand = support, a standing-by.

sentences.t: „Was verlangst du dafür?“ fragte der Jüngling.
sentences.l: “What do you ask for it?” asked the youth.

sentences.t: „Wenn wir dort in den Wald kommen, so schieß mich todt und hau mir Kopf und Pfoten ab.“
sentences.l: “When we come into the wood over there, then shoot me dead and hew off my head and paws.”
sentences.i: “When we come into the wood over there, shoot me dead and cut off my head and paws.”
sentences.n: todt = modern tot. “abhauen” = to hew off, and mir is a dative of possession: hew the head and paws off me. The tale means it literally, and the fox will ask twice.

sentences.t: „Das wäre eine schöne Dankbarkeit,“ sagte der Königssohn, „das kann ich dir unmöglich gewähren.“
sentences.l: “That would be a fine gratitude,” said the king’s son, “that I can impossibly grant you.”
sentences.i: “That would be a fine sort of gratitude,” said the king’s son; “I could not possibly grant you that.”
sentences.n: “eine schöne Dankbarkeit” is bitter irony — a fine thanks that would be. unmöglich stands adverbially: not possibly.

sentences.t: Sprach der Fuchs „wenn du es nicht thun willst, so muß ich dich verlassen; ehe ich aber fortgehe, will ich dir noch einen guten Rath geben.
sentences.l: Spoke the fox “if you will not do it, then I must leave you; but before I go away, I will give you one more good piece of counsel.
sentences.i: Said the fox: “If you will not do it, then I must leave you; but before I go, I will give you one more piece of good advice.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with its verb — “Sprach der Fuchs” — a brisk narrative speech tag. ehe = before, as a conjunction.

sentences.t: Vor zwei Stücken hüte dich, kauf kein Galgenfleisch und setze dich an keinen Brunnenrand.“
sentences.l: Guard yourself against two things: buy no gallows-flesh and set yourself on no well-rim.”
sentences.i: Guard yourself against two things: buy no gallows-flesh, and sit on no well-rim.”
sentences.n: Stück here is simply a thing, an item. Galgenfleisch — “gallows-flesh”: a man already under sentence of hanging, whom one might buy free. Both warnings come true exactly.

sentences.t: Damit lief er in den Wald.
sentences.l: With that he ran into the forest.
sentences.n: damit here is the pronominal adverb — with that, at that — not the conjunction “so that”; as a conjunction it would send the verb to the end.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling dachte „das ist ein wunderliches Thier, das seltsame Grillen hat.
sentences.l: The youth thought “that is a strange animal, which has odd whims.
sentences.i: The youth thought: “That is an odd creature, with strange notions in his head.
sentences.n: “Grillen haben” — literally to have crickets: to be full of whims and fancies.

sentences.t: Wer wird Galgenfleisch kaufen! und die Lust mich an einen Brunnenrand zu setzen ist mir noch niemals gekommen.“
sentences.l: Who will buy gallows-flesh! and the desire to set myself on a well-rim has never yet come to me.”
sentences.i: Who would buy gallows-flesh! And the wish to sit on a well-rim has never yet come over me.”
sentences.n: The 1857 text runs straight on after the exclamation mark with a lower-case und — we keep the original. “die Lust kommt mir” = the desire comes over me.

sentences.t: Er ritt mit der schönen Jungfrau weiter, und sein Weg führte ihn wieder durch das Dorf, in welchem seine beiden Brüder geblieben waren.
sentences.l: He rode on with the beautiful maiden, and his way led him again through the village in which his two brothers had stayed.
sentences.n: “in welchem” for in dem — welcher as a relative pronoun is the more formal choice, and the tales reach for it when a sentence is already long.

sentences.t: Da war großer Auflauf und Lärmen, und als er fragte was da vor wäre, hieß es, es sollten zwei Leute aufgehängt werden.
sentences.l: There was a great crowd and clamour, and when he asked what was going on there, it was said two people were to be hanged.
sentences.i: There was a great crowd and uproar; and when he asked what was afoot, he was told that two men were to be hanged.
sentences.n: “was vor wäre” — from vorsein, to be going on. “es hieß” = the word was, it was said. Auflauf is a running-together of people, a throng.

sentences.t: Als er näher hinzu kam, sah er daß es seine Brüder waren, die allerhand schlimme Streiche verübt und all ihr Gut verthan hatten.
sentences.l: When he came nearer up, he saw that it was his brothers, who had committed all manner of wicked tricks and squandered all their goods.
sentences.i: When he came nearer, he saw that it was his brothers, who had played all manner of wicked tricks and squandered everything they had.
sentences.n: verthan is from verthun (modern vertun), to waste, to squander.

sentences.t: Er fragte ob sie nicht könnten frei gemacht werden.
sentences.l: He asked whether they could not be made free.
sentences.i: He asked whether they could not be set free.
sentences.n: ob = whether, an indirect question. The order is the older one: könnten stands ahead of “frei gemacht werden”, where modern German would close the clause with the modal.

sentences.t: „Wenn ihr für sie bezahlen wollt,“ antworteten die Leute, „aber was wollt ihr an die schlechten Menschen euer Geld hängen und sie loskaufen.“
sentences.l: “If you will pay for them,” answered the people, “but why do you want to hang your money on the bad people and buy them free.”
sentences.i: “If you are willing to pay for them,” answered the people — “but why should you hang your money on such worthless men and buy them free?”
sentences.n: ihr is the plural you the crowd uses to a stranger. “Geld an etwas hängen” = to lay out money on a thing. The 1857 text ends this question with a full stop; we keep it.

sentences.t: Er besann sich aber nicht, zahlte für sie, und als sie frei gegeben waren, so setzten sie die Reise gemeinschaftlich fort.
sentences.l: But he did not reflect, paid for them, and when they had been set free, they continued the journey in common.
sentences.i: But he did not stop to think; he paid for them, and when they had been set free they all continued the journey together.
sentences.n: “sich besinnen” = to reflect, to think twice. gemeinschaftlich = in common, in company.

sentences.t: Sie kamen in den Wald, wo ihnen der Fuchs zuerst begegnet war, und da es darin kühl und lieblich war, und die Sonne heiß brannte, so sagten die beiden Brüder „laßt uns hier an dem Brunnen ein wenig ausruhen, essen und trinken.“
sentences.l: They came into the wood where the fox had first met them, and since it was cool and lovely in there, and the sun burned hot, the two brothers said “let us rest a little here by the well, eat and drink.”
sentences.i: They came into the wood where the fox had first met them; and since it was cool and pleasant inside while the sun burned hot, the two brothers said: “Let us rest a little here by the well, and eat and drink.”
sentences.n: da here = since, because.

sentences.t: Er willigte ein, und während des Gesprächs vergaß er sich, setzte sich an den Brunnenrand und versah sich nichts arges.
sentences.l: He agreed, and during the conversation he forgot himself, set himself on the well-rim and suspected nothing bad.
sentences.i: He agreed; and in the course of the talk he forgot himself, sat down on the rim of the well, and suspected no harm.
sentences.n: “sich versehen” with a genitive = to expect, to be on one’s guard against; “nichts arges” = nothing evil (modern nichts Arges). “einwilligen” = to consent.

sentences.t: Aber die beiden Brüder warfen ihn rückwärts in den Brunnen, nahmen die Jungfrau, das Pferd und den Vogel, und zogen heim zu ihrem Vater.
sentences.l: But the two brothers threw him backwards into the well, took the maiden, the horse and the bird, and went home to their father.

sentences.t: „Da bringen wir nicht bloß den goldenen Vogel,“ sagten sie, „wir haben auch das goldene Pferd und die Jungfrau von dem goldenen Schlosse erbeutet.“
sentences.l: “Here we bring not merely the golden bird,” they said, “we have also taken as booty the golden horse and the maiden from the golden castle.”
sentences.i: “Here we bring not only the golden bird,” they said; “we have carried off the golden horse and the maiden from the golden castle as well.”
sentences.n: erbeuten = to take as booty — the brothers’ own word gives them away.

sentences.t: Da war große Freude, aber das Pferd das fraß nicht, der Vogel der pfiff nicht, und die Jungfrau die saß und weinte.
sentences.l: There was great joy, but the horse, that one did not eat, the bird, that one did not whistle, and the maiden, that one sat and wept.
sentences.i: There was great rejoicing — but the horse would not eat, the bird would not whistle, and the maiden sat and wept.
sentences.n: Each subject is picked up by a pointing das/der/die before its verb, a rocking rhythm that sets the three sorrows side by side. fressen is the verb used of animals eating.

sentences.t: Der jüngste Bruder war aber nicht umgekommen.
sentences.l: But the youngest brother had not perished.

sentences.t: Der Brunnen war zum Glück trocken, und er fiel auf weiches Moos ohne Schaden zu nehmen, konnte aber nicht wieder heraus.
sentences.l: The well was luckily dry, and he fell on soft moss without taking harm, but could not get out again.
sentences.i: Luckily the well was dry, and he fell on soft moss without taking any harm; but he could not get out again.
sentences.n: “Schaden nehmen” = to take harm. In “konnte aber nicht wieder heraus” the verb of motion is left out after the modal — could not [get] out again.

sentences.t: Auch in dieser Noth verließ ihn der treue Fuchs nicht, kam zu ihm herabgesprungen und schalt ihn daß er seinen Rath vergessen hätte.
sentences.l: Even in this distress the faithful fox did not forsake him, came springing down to him and scolded him that he had forgotten his advice.
sentences.i: Even in this distress the faithful fox did not forsake him: he came springing down to him, and scolded him for having forgotten his advice.
sentences.n: “kam… herabgesprungen” — a participle after kommen tells the manner of the arrival. hätte is subjunctive: the reproach is reported, not asserted.

sentences.t: „Ich kanns aber doch nicht lassen,“ sagte er, „ich will dir wieder an das Tageslicht helfen.“
sentences.l: “And yet I cannot let it be,” he said, “I will help you back to the daylight.”
sentences.i: “And yet I cannot leave it alone,” he said; “I will help you back into the daylight.”
sentences.n: “es nicht lassen können” = to be unable to refrain from it. kanns = kann es.

sentences.t: Er sagte ihm er sollte seinen Schwanz anpacken und sich fest daran halten, und zog ihn dann in die Höhe.
sentences.l: He told him he should take hold of his tail and hold himself fast to it, and then pulled him up into the height.
sentences.i: He told him to take hold of his tail and hold fast to it, and then drew him up.
sentences.n: “in die Höhe” = up, into the air. anpacken = to grab hold of.

sentences.t: „Noch bist du nicht aus aller Gefahr,“ sagte der Fuchs, „deine Brüder waren deines Todes nicht gewis und haben den Wald mit Wächtern umstellt, die sollen dich tödten, wenn du dich sehen ließest.“
sentences.l: “You are not yet out of all danger,” said the fox, “your brothers were not certain of your death and have surrounded the wood with watchmen, who are to kill you if you let yourself be seen.”
sentences.i: “You are not yet out of all danger,” said the fox. “Your brothers were not sure you were dead, and have set watchmen all round the wood, who are to kill you if you let yourself be seen.”
sentences.n: gewis (modern gewiß/gewiss) takes the genitive: “deines Todes gewis”, sure of your death. ließest is subjunctive; tödten = modern töten.

sentences.t: Da saß ein armer Mann am Weg, mit dem vertauschte der Jüngling die Kleider und gelangte auf diese Weise an des Königs Hof.
sentences.l: There sat a poor man by the way; with him the youth exchanged the clothes and reached in this manner the king’s court.
sentences.i: A poor man was sitting by the road; with him the youth exchanged clothes, and in this way came to the king’s court.
sentences.n: “des Königs Hof” — the genitive placed before its noun, an elevated old order.

sentences.t: Niemand erkannte ihn, aber der Vogel fieng an zu pfeifen, das Pferd fieng an zu fressen, und die schöne Jungfrau hörte Weinens auf.
sentences.l: Nobody recognized him, but the bird began to whistle, the horse began to eat, and the beautiful maiden left off her weeping.
sentences.n: aufhören normally takes mit or zu; here the older genitive “Weinens” does the work — ceased of weeping. The three signs answer the three sorrows a page earlier.

sentences.t: Der König fragte verwundert „was hat das zu bedeuten?“
sentences.l: The king asked in wonder “what is that to mean?”
sentences.i: The king asked in wonder: “What is the meaning of this?”
sentences.n: “was hat das zu bedeuten” is the set question for what a thing means. verwundert is a past participle doing an adverb’s work: in wonder.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Jungfrau „ich weiß es nicht, aber ich war so traurig und nun bin ich so fröhlich.
sentences.l: Then the maiden spoke “I do not know it, but I was so sad and now I am so glad.

sentences.t: Es ist mir, als wäre mein rechter Bräutigam gekommen.“
sentences.l: It is to me as if my right bridegroom had come.”
sentences.i: I feel as though my true bridegroom had come.”
sentences.n: “es ist mir, als…” = I feel as if…; recht here = true, rightful. wäre is the subjunctive after als, as if.

sentences.t: Sie erzählte ihm alles was geschehen war, obgleich die andern Brüder ihr den Tod angedroht hatten, wenn sie etwas verrathen würde.
sentences.l: She told him everything that had happened, although the other brothers had threatened her with death if she should betray anything.
sentences.i: She told him everything that had happened, although the other brothers had threatened her with death if she betrayed a word of it.
sentences.n: “jemandem den Tod androhen” = to threaten someone with death, the person in the dative. verrathen = modern verraten.

sentences.t: Der König hieß alle Leute vor sich bringen, die in seinem Schloß waren, da kam auch der Jüngling als ein armer Mann in seinen Lumpenkleidern, aber die Jungfrau erkannte ihn gleich und fiel ihm um den Hals.
sentences.l: The king bade all the people who were in his castle be brought before him; then the youth came too, as a poor man in his rag-clothes, but the maiden recognized him at once and fell about his neck.
sentences.i: The king ordered all the people in his castle to be brought before him; and the youth came too, as a poor man in his rags — but the maiden knew him at once and fell on his neck.
sentences.n: heißen here = to bid, to order, with a bare infinitive (“bringen”). “jemandem um den Hals fallen” = to throw one’s arms round someone’s neck.

sentences.t: Die gottlosen Brüder wurden ergriffen und hingerichtet, er aber ward mit der schönen Jungfrau vermählt und zum Erben des Königs bestimmt.
sentences.l: The godless brothers were seized and executed, but he was wedded to the beautiful maiden and appointed heir of the king.
sentences.i: The godless brothers were seized and put to death, while he was married to the beautiful maiden and named the king’s heir.
sentences.n: The 1857 text does not soften the brothers’ end. “zum Erben bestimmen” = to designate as heir.

sentences.t: Aber wie ist es dem armen Fuchs ergangen?
sentences.l: But how has it gone for the poor fox?
sentences.i: But how did it fare with the poor fox?
sentences.n: The narrator turns to the reader in the present tense — and does so to open a last scene rather than to close the tale.

sentences.t: Lange danach gieng der Königssohn einmal wieder in den Wald, da begegnete ihm der Fuchs und sagte „du hast nun alles, was du dir wünschen kannst, aber mit meinem Unglück will es kein Ende nehmen, und es steht doch in deiner Macht mich zu erlösen,“
sentences.l: Long afterwards the king’s son went once more into the wood; there the fox met him and said “you have everything now that you can wish for yourself, but my misfortune will take no end, and yet it stands in your power to release me,”
sentences.i: Long afterwards the king’s son went once more into the wood, and there the fox met him and said: “Now you have everything you could wish for, but there is no end to my misfortune — and yet it lies in your power to release me,”
sentences.n: “es will kein Ende nehmen” — wollen of a thing means it simply does not, will not, come to an end. erlösen is the tales’ word for breaking an enchantment.

sentences.t: und abermals bat er flehentlich er möchte ihn todtschießen und ihm Kopf und Pfoten abhauen.
sentences.l: and again he begged imploringly that he might shoot him dead and hew off his head and paws.
sentences.i: and again he begged imploringly that the youth would shoot him dead and cut off his head and paws.
sentences.n: möchte is the subjunctive of the request as reported. The German leaves both parties as bare pronouns and lets the reader sort out who asks what of whom.

sentences.t: Also that ers, und kaum war es geschehen, so verwandelte sich der Fuchs in einen Menschen, und war niemand anders als der Bruder der schönen Königstochter, der endlich von dem Zauber, der auf ihm lag, erlöst war.
sentences.l: So he did it, and scarcely had it happened, then the fox transformed himself into a man, and was nobody other than the brother of the beautiful king’s daughter, who was at last released from the spell that lay upon him.
sentences.i: So he did it; and no sooner was it done than the fox turned into a man, and was none other than the brother of the beautiful king’s daughter, released at last from the spell that lay upon him.
sentences.n: “that ers” = that er es, with that the old spelling of tat. A spell in German lies on a person: “der Zauber, der auf ihm lag”.

sentences.t: Und nun fehlte nichts mehr zu ihrem Glück so lange sie lebten.
sentences.l: And now nothing more was wanting to their happiness so long as they lived.
sentences.n: “fehlen zu” = to be wanting for. The tale ends on the word it began with: at the opening an apple was missing every morning, and now nothing is missing at all.
